en: Slightly acidic rainwater dissolves the limestone rock of the Puerto Princesa Underground River over millions of years, carving out massive underground caverns.
Tiny coral polyps in Tubbataha Reef extract calcium from seawater to build hard limestone skeletons, slowly creating massive underwater reef structures.
Fast-flowing water in the Cagayan River slows down near the sea, dropping carried sediment to build a wide, fertile river delta.
Underground magma in Albay heats trapped groundwater into steam, which is piped to the surface to spin turbines and generate electricity.
Violent volcanic eruptions emptied the magma chamber beneath Batangas, causing the ground to collapse and fill with rainwater to form Lake Taal.
Ancient stone walls in the Banaue Rice Terraces hold soil and slow water runoff, preventing the steep mountain slopes from washing away.
Warm ocean waters in the Philippine Sea evaporate and rise, providing the heat energy that fuels and strengthens approaching tropical cyclones.
The Amihan wind picks up moisture from the Pacific Ocean and drops heavy rain on eastern Luzon when it hits the mountains.
The Philippine Trench forms where the Eurasian Plate subducts beneath the Philippine Sea Plate, releasing built-up underground stress as powerful earthquakes.
Dense forests in the Sierra Madre mountains absorb heavy typhoon rains, slowing water runoff and preventing severe flash floods in downstream cities.
The tangled roots of mangrove trees in Olango Island trap sediment and break strong waves, protecting the shoreline from coastal erosion.
Mineral-rich water dripping through the ceiling of Sumaguing Cave leaves behind tiny calcium deposits, slowly building downward-pointing rock formations called stalactites.
